review_status: Draft for clinical, pharmacy and patient/PPI review
title: Weekly paclitaxel

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Sensory or motor neuropathy, potentially persistent
Hair loss and nail / skin changes
Rare serious lung or cardiac effects

sources.title: eviQ: patient information (supportive explanation; NCCP schedule takes priority)
HSE: chemotherapy side effects and urgent advice

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

phases_note: The treating team confirms the indication, schedule and duration. Changes are recorded on your own prescription.
medicines_title: Your medicines and what they do
timeline_note: Bars show planned treatment and possible symptom patterns, not measured risk. Side effects can overlap and persist.
safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Act on fever, sudden illness or a new serious symptom whenever it occurs. Do not wait for the next appointment.
teachback: Can you explain which medicines you are receiving, the schedule, the contact plan and the symptoms that need prompt help?
consent_support: Confirm the indication, weekly schedule, hypersensitivity premedication, neuropathy assessment and any required off-label-use discussion.
urgent_extra: New chest pain, breathing difficulty, severe diarrhoea, inability to drink, reduced urine, uncontrolled bleeding or a rapidly worsening symptom needs prompt assessment.

chapters.title: Which cancer setting does this page cover?
chapters.intro: The regimen number matters as well as the drug name.

items.title: Advanced breast cancer
items.text: The NCCP indication concerns metastatic breast cancer after unsuitable or unsuccessful anthracycline-based treatment. Tumour biology and previous treatments influence options. This page does not describe every early-breast-cancer paclitaxel regimen.

items.title: Ovarian, small-cell lung and bladder cancer
items.text: These are specific later-line settings in this shared protocol. Evidence is less robust than for the breast-cancer weekly comparison. Ask about current alternatives and the implications of use outside the licensed indication where applicable.

items.title: Paclitaxel formulations and combinations
items.text: Conventional paclitaxel and nab-paclitaxel have different formulations and administration requirements. This is a single-agent paclitaxel guide. If another anti-cancer medicine is added, obtain the matching combination guide.

items.title: What matters to you?
items.text: Discuss symptom control, time in hospital, hair loss, neuropathy risk and the activities you most want to preserve. Your priorities can change. Supportive care is available alongside active treatment.

chapters.title: Before each weekly visit
chapters.intro: Use the time between appointments to make review more informative.

items.title: Write down change from your baseline
items.text: Record tingling, numbness, pain, balance, bowel symptoms and fatigue. Tell the team about fever or illness when it occurs; the record is not a reason to wait.

items.title: Check medicines and transport
items.text: Know whether premedication is taken at home or given in hospital. Bring your medicine list and tell the team about a previous infusion reaction. Sedating antihistamines can affect driving.

items.title: Know the agreed schedule
items.text: Check the planned treatment days and blood-test arrangements. A three-visit and four-visit schedule must be distinguished in your own prescription. The number of visits may change after clinical review.

chapters.title: What the checks are for
chapters.intro: Symptoms, blood results and the treatment aim answer different questions.

items.title: Blood counts
items.text: Neutrophils protect against infection, haemoglobin carries oxygen and platelets help clotting. A normal previous result or feeling well does not prove the current counts are safe. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate advice.

items.title: Kidney and liver function
items.text: Organ function can change drug exposure. Vomiting or diarrhoea can cause dehydration and worsen kidney function. Report reduced urine, poor intake, jaundice and new medicines. The clinical assessment combines results with symptoms.

items.title: Describe symptoms in practical terms
items.text: Tell the team about the worst symptoms since the last visit, even if improved today. Examples include extra stools above your usual pattern, whether mouth pain affects drinking, and whether numbness affects buttons or balance.

items.title: Assessing cancer control
items.text: The review plan may use scans, symptoms and ability to manage daily life. Stable disease can be worthwhile. Ask what benefit would justify continuing and what alternatives would be considered if treatment stops helping.

chapters.title: What to watch for
chapters.intro: Some effects appear early; others build over repeated doses.

items.title: Neuropathy and lasting effects
items.text: Paclitaxel can affect sensation and sometimes strength. Report numbness, burning pain, weakness or difficulty with everyday tasks before the next dose. Symptoms may take time to improve and can persist after treatment.

items.title: Aches and fatigue
items.text: Muscle or joint pain can occur after treatment. Use the agreed analgesia plan and describe how pain affects sleep and function. New extreme weakness, fainting or breathlessness should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to treatment.

items.title: Hair, skin and nails
items.text: Hair loss is common with paclitaxel; it may include body hair. Nail changes and skin symptoms can occur. Ask about practical support and report painful, infected or rapidly worsening changes.

items.title: Mouth, bowels and infection
items.text: Gentle mouth care and early reporting help when soreness affects eating. Report persistent diarrhoea or vomiting. Low blood counts can make infection dangerous; a normal temperature does not make sudden illness safe.

items.title: Infusion and breathing symptoms
items.text: Reactions can occur during infusion despite premedication. Tell the nurse immediately. New cough or breathlessness after leaving also needs assessment; the cause may be infection, a clot, treatment or cancer.

chapters.title: Living with treatment
chapters.intro: Plan around the activities and people that matter to you.

items.title: Food, drink and practical help
items.text: Use foods and drinks you can manage. Tell the team about weight loss, poor intake or difficulty shopping and cooking; ask for dietitian or practical support. A fixed daily fluid target is not appropriate for everyone, particularly with heart or kidney problems.

items.title: Activity, rest and driving
items.text: Balance rest with manageable activity. Record what fatigue stops you doing. Do not drive when dizzy, unwell or affected by sedating medicines. Ask about work adjustments and transport for treatment days.

items.title: Medicines, vaccines and supplements
items.text: Bring a complete medicine list, including over-the-counter products and supplements. Ask the oncology pharmacist before changes. Discuss vaccination timing. Do not stop prescribed long-term medicines on your own.

items.title: Fertility, contraception and breastfeeding
items.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment when relevant. Ask for a written contraception and breastfeeding plan covering each medicine and the period after treatment. Tell the team promptly about a possible pregnancy.

items.title: Support for you and your family
items.text: Ask about psycho-oncology, social work, counselling and symptom support. Take information in manageable amounts. A family member or trusted person can help record questions if you wish. Discuss how treatment fits your priorities.

chapters.title: Useful treatment terms
chapters.intro: Short explanations for the clinic conversation.

items.title: Taxane and microtubule
items.text: A taxane is a chemotherapy drug family. Microtubules are small cell structures involved in division and other functions. Effects on these structures help explain both anti-cancer activity and nerve toxicity.

items.title: Premedication and neuropathy
items.text: Premedication is medicine given before an infusion to reduce reactions. Neuropathy means nerve dysfunction. These are separate issues and both need review during weekly therapy.

purpose: This weekly paclitaxel protocol is used in specified advanced breast, ovarian, small-cell lung and bladder-cancer settings. The aim is usually disease control and symptom relief. Evidence and alternatives differ between cancers; confirm the indication with your oncologist.
schedule_summary: Paclitaxel on Days 1, 8, 15 and 22 of a 28-day cycle; a Days 1, 8 and 15 schedule may be selected by the consultant. Confirm your appointment plan.

phases.label: Days 1, 8, 15 and 22
phases.detail: Four weekly infusion visits within each 28-day cycle. The team reviews safety before each planned dose.

phases.label: Days 1, 8 and 15 (if prescribed)
phases.detail: Day 22 is omitted only if the three-visit schedule is prescribed. Follow your confirmed appointments and prescription.

timeline.label: Blood counts / energy
timeline.text: Review before each dose; report illness any day

day_groups.title: First visit of this cycle
day_groups.body: Review symptoms, blood results and premedication before the infusion. Tell the nurse straight away about itching, flushing, throat or chest tightness, back pain, dizziness or breathing change.
day_groups.action: Check transport if premedication makes you drowsy and confirm the next weekly visit.

day_groups.title: Between weekly doses
day_groups.body: Aches, fatigue, nausea or bowel symptoms may occur. Tingling may be mild at first but matters before the next dose. Record what symptoms stop you doing.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for new or worsening numbness, balance trouble, marked weakness or uncontrolled symptoms. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact.

day_groups.title: Second weekly review
day_groups.body: This dose requires its own symptom and blood-test review. Describe the worst symptoms since the previous visit, not only how you feel today.
day_groups.action: Report sensory changes before the infusion and confirm your premedication instructions.

day_groups.title: Keep tracking function
day_groups.body: Repeated treatment can increase nerve symptoms and fatigue. Check practical tasks such as buttons, writing and walking. Use the symptom passport to show changes.
day_groups.action: Seek early advice rather than waiting until numbness is severe.

day_groups.title: Third weekly review
day_groups.body: The team decides whether treatment can proceed using the current assessment.
day_groups.action: Confirm whether Day 22 is planned for you; do not infer this from a different person’s calendar.

day_groups.title: After the third visit
day_groups.body: Symptoms may settle or continue. An interval between appointments does not rule out infection or a treatment complication.
day_groups.action: Use the urgent contact plan if unwell and bring your record to the next review.

day_groups.title: Day 22: follow the prescribed schedule
day_groups.body: A fourth dose is part of the four-visit plan. In the consultant-selected three-visit plan there is no Day 22 infusion. The calendar here is educational.
day_groups.action: Use your confirmed appointment and prescription; call if the schedule is unclear.

day_groups.title: Complete the cycle record
day_groups.body: Record symptoms and functional changes, including those that improve before the next appointment. Treatment continuation depends on benefit, toxicity and your priorities.
day_groups.action: Check the next cycle date and review plan. Do not treat a gap in visits as a guarantee of recovery.

support.title: Premedication for infusion reactions
support.text: Steroid and antihistamine premedication reduce the chance or severity of reactions. The team may adjust premedication after tolerated doses. Do not omit or change it yourself; tell the nurse about missed doses.

support.title: Aches, nausea and bowel support
support.text: Agree a pain-relief and anti-sickness plan. Ask before taking new medicines. Uncontrolled pain or poor intake needs review. Some supportive medicines cause constipation or drowsiness.

support.title: Nerve symptoms and fall prevention
support.text: Use secure footwear and take care with balance, hot surfaces and sharp objects if sensation is reduced. Tell the team early about functional changes; persistent neuropathy may influence dosing.

support.title: Hair, nails and skin
support.text: Ask about hair-loss support and whether scalp cooling is appropriate and available. Protect sensitive nails and skin. Report painful nail changes, spreading rash, blistering or infection.

evidence.title: What supports the weekly schedule?
evidence.intro: This numerical comparison is for metastatic breast cancer, not the other indications.
evidence.population: CALGB 9840 compared weekly with three-weekly paclitaxel in metastatic breast cancer, with trastuzumab use linked to HER2 status and trial allocation.
evidence.interpretation: Weekly treatment had a higher response rate and more severe sensory neuropathy. This older trial is not an individual forecast or evidence for identical benefit across ovarian, small-cell lung and bladder cancer. The clinical knowledge base separates the evidence by indication.

chronology_notes.title: Weekly visits
chronology_notes.text: Each planned infusion needs its own symptom and blood-test review.

chronology_notes.title: Day 22
chronology_notes.text: The fourth visit applies only to the four-visit plan. Some patients are prescribed Days 1, 8 and 15; follow your confirmed schedule.

chronology_notes.title: Nerves and aches
chronology_notes.text: Aches can follow treatment; numbness, tingling and fatigue may persist or accumulate. Describe changes before the next dose.

chronology_notes.title: Blood counts
chronology_notes.text: A gap between visits does not exclude infection or another treatment complication. Fever or sudden illness needs immediate contact.
